strengths: The paper addresses a useful computational problem with a well-motivated combination of adversarial sample generation, bootstrapped targets, and learned Sinkhorn initialization. The predictions can be refined using ordinary Sinkhorn iterations, making the approach practically compatible with existing solvers.

The Hilbert projective loss appropriately handles the additive ambiguity of log-potentials. Proposition 4.3 provides a sound fixed-point residual bound for positive kernels, supporting the use of approximate targets without requiring fully converged training labels.

The reported improvements are substantial within the evaluated setting. At marginal constraint violation 0.01, Table 2 reports reductions from 47 to 3 iterations on CIFAR and from 41 to 4 on LFW; the Gaussian initialization requires 17 and 14 iterations, respectively. Evaluation across four unseen image datasets and five independent training runs provides meaningful evidence of transfer.

The algorithms and appendix describe the architecture and main hyperparameters, and a code repository is provided. The comparison against training on noise supplies useful evidence that the learned generator improves prediction quality.
weaknesses: The central universality claim exceeds the evidence. Theorem 4.1 assumes equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constraint, whereas the implemented generator maps a 392-dimensional latent input to two 784-dimensional distributions and does not enforce that constraint. The authors acknowledge these differences but still invoke the theorem to rule out generator coverage limitations. Moreover, full support would not establish uniform prediction accuracy. Four image datasets demonstrate useful transfer, but not reliable approximation of arbitrary distribution pairs even within the fixed cost and dimension.

Theorem 4.1 also requires mathematical correction. ReLU makes q noninvertible on the boundary and creates singular probability mass, so the stated density and inverse formula cannot hold throughout the closed nonnegative orthant. For example, with one dimension and net equal to zero, q has probability one-half at zero. Appendix A cannot discard ReLU without qualification, and Lipschitz continuity only guarantees differentiability almost everywhere. An interior, almost-everywhere formulation appears repairable, but would still not establish universality of the implemented generator.

The closest learned baseline, Amos et al. (2022), is excluded on the asserted grounds that it fails out of distribution, without presenting that comparison. This leaves the claimed improvement over prior meta OT learning insufficiently demonstrated. Comparing its objective with the proposed loss under matched architectures, generated training samples, and compute would help separate the contributions of sampling and bootstrapping. The unqualified claim of being the first meta neural OT solver also needs reconciliation with this acknowledged prior work.

The transport-distance evaluation is internally inconsistent. Algorithm 1 returns the transport cost <C, Gamma>, while Section 5.2 defines the reference value as the minimum of Problem 3.3, which includes the entropy term. These quantities differ even at convergence. The paper must clarify which quantity is plotted and how accurately the reference solutions were computed before its few-percent error and standalone-solver claims can be assessed confidently. This concern does not negate the separately reported marginal-constraint improvements.

The practical efficiency evidence is narrower than the conclusions suggest. Figure 8 compares runtime only against the default initialization, omitting the Gaussian baseline, and evaluation uses batches of 500 at one resolution and regularization value. Prediction overhead at smaller batch sizes, training-cost amortization, and scaling remain unclear. The assertion of hyperparameter insensitivity is also unsupported by a sensitivity study. These limitations, together with the central theoretical and comparison gaps, make weak rejection more appropriate despite the promising warm-start results.
